2.text: by means of a fire-drill. Any remaining particles of the leg-joint are covered

3.text: with small pieces of sod; and a willow-twig, taken from those that were used

4.text: in tying the leg-joint to the cross-pole in the tent, is put on top of it. The

5.text: small mound of sod thus arranged is called “fireplace” (mêˊlhɪn). A few days

6.text: later the first change of the camp-site takes place, but it is not accompanied

7.text: by any particular ceremony. Some of the people merely build two fires in

8.text: front of the two ends of the corral, and cause the train of sledges to pass

10.text: In the second slaughtering, all the details concerning the killing of the

11.text: animals, arranging the sledges, painting with blood, etc., are repeated, but

12.text: are done more hurriedly. The meeting of the herd with shooting and shouting

13.text: is omitted. The guests gather and receive gifts in the same manner as was

14.text: described before, but the shamans do not practise their arts. The thanks-

15.text: giving ceremony is performed only the first time; neither are the races and

16.text: wrestling-matches repeated. Immediately after the second slaughtering, the

17.text: actual moving-about on the moss pastures and the winter life begin.

18.text: Winter Slaughtering. — Other slaughtering-sacrifices during the year

19.text: are less complicated and less important. The next one in point of time is

20.text: connected with the establishment of the permanent winter house. Two or

21.text: three reindeer are slaughtered; two usually being sacrificed to the dawn, and

22.text: one to the ground (notaˊs˙qa-vaˊɪrg̣ɪn).¹ The last-named sacrifice is laid by

23.text: the left side of the others, with its head pointed towards sunset.

24.text: About the time of the winter solstice the “feeding” of the star Pehiˊttin

25.text: is celebrated. Those who are living in winter-quarters begin by repeating

26.text: the last-mentioned sacrifice, and a few days later sacrifice to Pehiˊttin. Fat

27.text: bucks are selected for this purpose. Small “substitute” figures are made,

28.text: corresponding to the number of fire-drill boards; and round cakes of pounded

29.text: leaves are prepared. Tiny leather plates with tallow and blood-soup are

30.text: offered to the east, because about this time the star begins to rise in the east.

31.text: Some of the people also make a ceremonial fire for the star Pehiˊttin, and

33.text: Those who move about all winter celebrate the Pehiˊttin ceremonial in

34.text: a simpler way. They often postpone it until the middle of the first month

36.text: In the interval between the first and the second lunar months of the

37.text: Chukchee year, a sacrifice to the sun is performed, but with no new details.

38.text: The next sacrifice is made between the “first summer” (kɪˊtkɪtɪk) and the

39.text: “second summer” (aˊnok),² when the herd is being driven to summer pastures.

40.text: The ceremonial opens with the last moving of the tent in the season. The
